title: Four requests
intro:
*Five minutes. Commit before you look.*

Four requests arrive in the same week, each with a sympathetic requester and a real observation behind it.

**One of them is actually a training problem.** Find it.

artifacts.label: Request A
artifacts.body:
"Our new managers are terrible at giving difficult feedback. I've watched three of them avoid a performance conversation for a whole quarter. They need training on how to have hard conversations."

You talk to six of them. All six describe good feedback practice accurately and in detail. Four mention, unprompted, that a colleague gave direct critical feedback last year and it showed up in their own review as 'abrasive'.

artifacts.label: Request B
artifacts.body:
"Finance has rolled out the new procurement system and nobody can use it. Approvals are stuck, people are raising tickets, and two teams have gone back to the old spreadsheet. Can you build something?"

You watch four people attempt a purchase. Each one gets to the same screen (a cost-centre field with no lookup and no error message) and stops. Three of them tell you they've asked what to enter and never got an answer.

artifacts.label: Request C
artifacts.body:
"We've just moved the clinical documentation standard to the new regulatory format. Everyone's been told, we sent the guidance PDF, and error rates in the audit have gone *up*, not down. I don't know what else to do."

You sample twenty records. The errors are consistent and specific: three fields are being completed under the old convention, by people who are clearly trying to comply and applying the rule they already knew.

artifacts.label: Request D
artifacts.body:
"Engagement scores on 'my manager supports my development' dropped eleven points in the sales org. The VP wants a development-conversations workshop for all forty managers before the next cycle."

You look at the cut. The drop is entirely in two of nine teams. Both report to the same director. The other seven are flat or up.

reasoning:
**C is the training problem, and it's the only one.** Apply the money test: could those clinicians complete the new format correctly tomorrow for a large enough reward? No. They don't know the new convention. They are trying to comply and applying a rule they learned properly and were never taught to replace. That is a genuine knowledge gap, and instruction is the right instrument. Note what makes it credible: the errors are *consistent and specific*, which is the signature of people correctly applying the wrong rule rather than people not caring. Note also that the organization already 'communicated' it, a PDF isn't instruction, and the rising error rate is what happens when a new procedure is announced rather than taught.

**A is the classic willingness case, and the reason it's first.** Six for six can describe good feedback. The capability is present; the environment punishes using it. Build the workshop and you'll confirm what they know, tell them the organization thinks the problem is their skill, and generate an attendance record that buys the review-calibration problem eighteen months of quiet. The real intervention is upstream and it isn't yours alone.

**B is a tooling problem wearing a training request.** Four people stop at the same field, and the field has no lookup and no error message. Training people to work around a broken form is a real option, and it is the option that makes the broken form permanent — because once there's a workaround, the ticket to fix it drops down the backlog forever. This is the request most likely to be accepted by a helpful L&D function, because it's easy and everyone will be grateful.

**D is a management problem, and the data says so before you talk to anyone.** Nine teams, drop in two, both under one director. A workshop for forty managers treats a population for the behaviour of one, spends the sales org's goodwill, and leaves the director's teams exactly where they were. The tell is in the cut, which took two minutes to look at, and which nobody had looked at before the request was written.

The transferable test: **the request tells you what someone wants built; the observation underneath tells you what they saw.** In three of these four, ten minutes with the actual evidence relocates the problem entirely.
